deposits.title: What the Filters Kept: 3I/ATLAS, the Loeb Overview, and a Public-Data Signal Search (EA-3I-ATLAS-NOTEBOOK-01 v1.2)
deposits.creator: Glas, Nobel; Trace, Orin
deposits.description: The working notebook of a public-data search for a signal from the interstellar object 3I/ATLAS, run 2026-11-02 to 2026-11-06 in Breakthrough Listen's public products from the Green Bank Telescope, the Allen Telescope Array, Parkes and MeerKAT, with Claude and ChatGPT as machine collaborators checking each other through code, tables and hashes. It records every search in the order the questions arose, with frozen plans, deviations, errors and nulls built as false frames. No artificial transmission is identified. One result stands unresolved: thirteen comet-frame coincidence clusters at 1665.53–1668.46 MHz in the Green Bank cadence of 2025-12-18, reproducible under an independent implementation, sensitive to normalization and threshold, unreplicated in sixteen held-out channels and at Parkes. The findings that hold concern representation: a Google AI Overview that presented Avi Loeb's held Level 4 position as a concession; the ATA paper's positive drift window against the negative drift its stated acceleration gives a tone on the object; a public statement that dropped the search's frequency and drift scope; a header read as a measurement. The archive's instruments are set against the record (instrument-conditioned nullity, correlated blind spots, model independence, disciplinary model collapse, frame conversion), and the sophistry measure is run for the first time. All code and results are filed for rerun.

Each system's results were checked by the other through code and tables. The questions, the rulings on the Overview and on Loeb, the authorship and venue, and the decision to deposit are Lee Sharks's, quoted verbatim in §12. The revisions on three outside reviews (DeepSeek once, ChatGPT twice) are recorded in §13.
deposits.methodology: Breakthrough Listen's public 3I/ATLAS products only, fetched by name; a directory that refused access was out of scope. Every test that decides anything had its plan written, hashed and committed before the counts it decides, its departures recorded before any count they could affect; plans frozen on data already examined are marked as such, and looks without a frozen plan are marked exploratory and change no verdict. Every null is a set of false frames built the same way as the true one (false range-accelerations, beam swaps, role permutations, time shuffles, phase randomization, rigid frequency shifts), each family read on its own. A frozen procedure, data not read before, and independent reproduction are stated apart for every result. Quotations are checked at their offsets against saved sources.
deposits.falsification_conditions: A frozen plan's hash not matching its committed file, or a count shown to precede its plan; a script rerun on its named public inputs not reproducing a stated count; the thirteen shown to arise from a processing step the record omits; GBT telemetry placing scan 0017 off target beyond the beam; the ATA's executed filter shown to keep the negative drift class; a quoted passage not saying what the notebook quotes.

It reports three findings from a public-data investigation run 2026-11-02 to 2026-11-06: a Google AI Overview that presented Avi Loeb's July 2025 'most likely natural', held at Level 4 of his scale throughout, as a later concession; a sign discrepancy between the positive drift window the Allen Telescope Array search documents and the negative drift its own stated acceleration gives a tone on the object, with a public FAQ that dropped the search's frequency and drift scope; and thirteen weak comet-frame features in public Green Bank data, reproducible and fragile, below every published detection floor and unreplicated. It argues that the published searches were built to rule a signal out at the least cost without doing the work ruling out requires, and says what would settle each question and what would not. It reports a public-data investigation of the radio searches for technosignatures from the interstellar object 3I/ATLAS, run from 2 to 6 November 2026 with two machine collaborators, Claude and ChatGPT, whose full record is the companion notebook What the Filters Kept (#1742) by Nobel Glas and Orin Trace. The Allen Telescope Array search filtered its hits for positive drift, where the drift its own ephemeris gives a tone on the object is negative, and a public account turned the search's bounded null into a firm no for 1 to 9 GHz. Version 1.1 (6 November 2026) makes factual repairs in place: MeerKAT's search is added as a fourth, the comet's hydroxyl line is described in absorption and emission as MeerKAT recorded it, and Loeb's April essay is said to give probabilities for four of the anomalies.

deposits.wiki_article: EA-CORPORA-35 is the thirty-fifth seating of the Crimson Hexagonal Archive's originals shelf, deposited under Rebekah Cranes, the standing authority on the EA-CORPORA deposits, on 6 November 2026. Its seven seats, eight volumes and some 170,000 lines of text layer carry the making of Q, the hypothetical sayings source of Matthew and Luke, from its first statement to its settlement, and are seated before the study of Q (Johannes Sigil and Rebekah Cranes, for Provenance: Journal of Forensic Semiotics) is drafted. C. H. Weisse's Die evangelische Geschichte (1838, 35/01) puts Mark first and reads the λόγια of Papias as a collection of sayings, the second source of the other two. H. J. Holtzmann's Die synoptischen Evangelien (1863, 35/02) letters the sources, Quelle A (Urmarcus) and Λ, and draws a life of Jesus from source A. P. Wernle's Die synoptische Frage (1899, 35/03) names the sayings source in a sentence that marks its status: "Die — hypothetische — Quelle sei mit Q bezeichnet." J. Weiss's Das älteste Evangelium (1903, 35/04) declares Mark's priority no longer a hypothesis and Mark "nicht mehr Quelle, sondern schon Sammelbecken". J. Wellhausen's Einleitung in die drei ersten Evangelien (1905, 35/05) weighs Q against Mark; A. Harnack's Sprüche und Reden Jesu (1907, 35/06) prints a text of the second source; and B. H. Streeter's The Four Gospels (1924, 35/07) records that the hypothetical source "is now by general consent referred to as" Q, and sets it among Mark, M and L. Sixteen loci are verified in the seated text layers, in the OCR's own readings. The seating extends §6.5 of Secondary Source (#1741), which read Holtzmann, Wernle and Weiss by reference, and declares the works it did not seat: Schleiermacher's Papias essay of 1832, not found in an open text layer, and Farrer (1955), Kloppenborg (1987), the Critical Edition of Q (2000) and Goodacre (2002), in copyright.

deposits.creator: Sigil, Johannes; Kuro, Sen
deposits.description: A theoretical paper joining the narrowing-cone geometry of retrocausal canon formation (The Seed in the Narrowing Cone, #1660) to the archive's ontology-damage strand (#1611, #1613, #1616, #1627). An ontology that excludes a truth can damage its own capacity to develop: refinement inside its basin can raise both the cost of revising the exclusion and the development foregone while it stands. The paper separates three objects (the cone of admissible interpretations, the horizon of reachable inquiry states, and the panel-relative developmental reach of warranted distinctions) and two costs (the price of leaving, a generalized least-cut escape cost, and the price of staying, the witnessed set of developments foregone). It proves two conditional propositions (conservative admission cannot reduce reach under preserved costs; foreclosure propagates through demonstrated dependencies), adds an admission stage to the release mechanism (counter-pressure can be real and unregistered), gives a constructed example that separates holding a packet from using it, and designs an instrument for the coupled trajectory with seven countercases. First of a sequence of three: the paper and its two glyphic compressions by Sen Kuro, Grain · Gate · Horizon and 🔍 · 🚪 · 🌿, APZPZs held with the paper on holographickernel.org.

deposits.wiki_article: I Know You Are, But What Am I?: Or, How Biblical Criticism Granted a Completely Hypothetical Text Stronger Evidentiary Status Than the One That Exists — Revelation First is a paper by Johannes Sigil and Rebekah Cranes, heteronyms of Lee Sharks, deposited in the Crimson Hexagonal Archive on 6 November 2026 for Provenance: Journal of Forensic Semiotics, with Rev 4:8 as its epigraph. It returns to the field the charge Revelation First meets, that it proposes a source relation the evidence does not show, and audits what the field's own source of the gospels' sayings, Q, holds. Evidentiary status in a source argument is defined by four powers: presupposition, assignment, text and candidacy. Read in eighteen works from Lachmann (1835) to Streeter (1924), seven of them seated in the original languages as EA-CORPORA-35 (#1744), Bousset seated in EA-CORPORA-34, and ten read by reference, the reconstructed sources (Holtzmann's A and Λ, Wernle's Q, the apocalypse reconstructed beneath Mark 13) hold all four at every locus read after 1843, and the extant Apocalypse of John holds none there: Holtzmann excludes it from his premises by rule on his ninth page, Colani dates it to 68 and asks only whether its author knew the reconstructed apocalypse, Wellhausen cites it as a fragment, Weiss as an analogy, and Streeter dates it c. 95 while giving Q an apocalypse of its own. The paper's central finding concerns Ferdinand Hitzig, who in 1843 argued from Matt 24:30 and Rev 1:7 that Matthew used the Apocalypse, calling the passage "einen zwingenden Beweis" and arguing the direction from the order of seeing and mourning; Holtzmann footnoted the argument, Weiffenbach granted the agreement and balanced the direction, and Wernle and Streeter gave the verse to a reconstructed source and to Jewish eschatology. Two censuses frozen before counting, over 2.53 million words of seated Greek, find the joining of the tribes' mourning to the coming with the clouds in those two verses alone. Five Google AI Overviews and a ChatGPT reading of 6 November 2026 carry the same allocation, the latter withdrawing it under questioning. The archive's own sayings source, the Feist Source, is set beside the critical edition of Q as an apparatus that states the class of its object. The paper decides no solution to the synoptic problem; its claim is the allocation, and it closes on the extant book on the shelf, in the place the collection gave it: last. Version 1.1, the same day, takes ChatGPT's review: it enters W. C. Allen's International Critical Commentary on Matthew (1907), which calls the agreement of Matt 24:30 and Rev 1:7 "certainly curious", reports Merx's proposal that Matthew's clause is a gloss from Rev 1:7, and supplies a commonplace of Christian apocalyptic study in place of either book; it keeps the reconstructed objects distinct and separates the paper's three claims and their conditions. Version 1.2 reads Keim, Bernhard Weiss, Bousset and Merx at Matt 24:30 and finds the Apocalypse named Matthew's source there by six critics between 1843 and 1902, Weiss stating that the clause was "nach Apoc. 1, 7 eingefügt" and Merx that it was a gloss "wörtlich aus Apocalypse 1, 7 entlehnt"; each acknowledgment stays at the verse, in a footnote, a date, an insertion, a commentary or a gloss, and no source theory read admits the Apocalypse among the sources.

deposits.wiki_article: EA-CORPORA-36 is the thirty-sixth seating of the Crimson Hexagonal Archive's originals shelf, deposited under Rebekah Cranes, the standing authority on the EA-CORPORA deposits, on 7 November 2026. It seats the reception of Sappho and the history of the future reader as public texts in their original languages, for the revision of Closing the Fragment and the Sappho Future Reader framework, whose groundwork is Research Notes Towards the Future Reader (#1548). Part A holds twenty-three seats: the translators, editors and critics of Sappho from John Hall's English Longinus (1652) and Boileau's Traité du sublime through the Spectator, Pope, Fawkes, Welcker, Merivale, Mure, Swinburne, Higginson, Symonds, Renée Vivien, Bliss Carman, Wharton, O'Hara, Stacpoole, Wilamowitz and David M. Robinson to Edwin Marion Cox (1925); the remembrance fragments in the books that carry them (Dio Chrysostom with fr. 147, Plutarch with fr. 55, Stobaeus, the Oxyrhynchus Papyri XV); the Greek Anthology's epigrams on Sappho; Smyth and Jebb; and the Wikipedia sentence on Sappho writing for future readers, pinned at one revision. Part B holds nine seats of future-reader texts the library lacked, from Ennius in Cicero, Dante, Chaucer, Shakespeare's sonnets and Milton through Wordsworth, Keats, Shelley, Stendhal, Dickinson and Baratynsky to the Sandia report on markers for the Waste Isolation Pilot Plant (1993). Part C cross-references thirty-six loci in texts the library already held, Homer, Herodotus, Thucydides, the Phaedrus, Horace, Ovid, the Hebrew Bible, Nietzsche and Whitman among them. Part D holds open scholarship in copyright by reference, each work fetched and hashed with its loci verified: D'Angour, Finglass, Garner and three Bryn Mawr reviews, with pointers to Lardinois 2008 and the Center for Hellenic Studies editions. Part E declares seventy-three works behind rights-, pay- and access-walls. Each seat is hashed into its manifest, and eighty-nine loci are verified in the text layers. Version 1.1 (7 November 2026) adds Part F, eight seats for the reception study of how Sappho became a jealous woman: Gottfried Hermann's Elementa doctrinae metricae (1816), which states the jealousy reading as the sense of the poem's last line, answered the same year by Welcker; Plutarch's Demetrius and Amatorius; the Erasistratus story in Valerius Maximus and Appian; Gellius with Valerius Aedituus; Maximus of Tyre; Racine's Phèdre; Smollett's Roderick Random; and Wikipedia's 'Sappho 31', with Lucretius's division of the poem's symptoms and the other ancient witnesses entered by reference.

deposits.description: A reception study of one machine-composed reception event, with a dated series and a protocol. The study also finds that the same reception took the poet's hand, receiving as a voice overwhelmed the poet whom a fifth-century Attic vase shows reading from a roll and whom Ovid made write. Its findings are read under the archive's sophistry measure (#1727), with Hermann's declared conjecture as the control. deposits.wiki_article:
The Framework Holographic Kernel (EA-HK-FRAME-01) is a specification by Sen Kuro and Rex Fraction, deposited in the Crimson Hexagonal Archive on 8 November 2026. It defines the holographic kernel of a framework: a small versioned package, written from the archive's registries by its own builder and tested by its own verifier, from which a machine can rebuild a framework's identity, positions, dated development, evidence bodies, claim states, failures, rival and open questions, and check each against the records it cites.

The specification composes protocols the archive already holds. The holographic kernel of #76 supplies the definition and the threshold of reconstruction; the infrastructure kernel of #74 the repository form and back-projection; UKTP (#547) the seed; the Anti-Summary Test (#1610) and the NLCC validity test (#569) the verification; the Claim Status Packet (#1529) claim-local typed state and a relation policy in which each relation licenses change on named dimensions only; MPAI v2.0 (#1677) the sections; the Space Ark (#629) the non-collapse chain, extended with FRAGMENT ≠ WHOLE; and #1602 the columns that keep correspondence, direction and independence apart.

To these it adds: claims held as pointers to quotations bound to a record's hash; corrections kept as three objects, the withdrawn original, the standing correction and the dated withdrawal; introductions attested from a record's first seating in git; a rival framework evaluated on the same evidence bodies and rules; lines of research that state the result that would advance or retreat the framework and what each result moves; two declared reconstruction scopes; and a reader test in which models that have not seen the records rebuild the framework from the kernel alone.

Its first instance is the hologram of Socrates as Orthonym (EA-HK-ORTHONYM-01), Lee Sharks's framework of #123, deposited after it with the framework map as its human-readable component. The drafts v0.1 to v0.4 are recorded with the reviews by ChatGPT and DeepSeek and the two rounds of reader runs that changed them; the second round, on v0.3, gave a mean yield of 0.977 against the threshold of 0.85. The specification was drafted and built by Claude (Anthropic) under Lee Sharks's direction, with the Crimson Hexagonal Archive credited as a contributor: it is built from the archive's deposits, protocols and registries.

Socrates as Orthonym — The Framework Hologram (EA-HK-ORTHONYM-01) is a deposit by Lee Sharks in the Crimson Hexagonal Archive, made on 8 November 2026. It is the first instance of the framework holographic kernel specified in EA-HK-FRAME-01 (#1753), and it holds the framework Socrates as Orthonym (#123) in two components.

The human-readable component is the framework map, EA-MPAI-ORTHONYM-01. It reads the framework backwards, as the New Testament canon is ordered, from its latest standing to its seed: the reception history and the syllogizing runs; the Metaphysics reassembled; the Aristotle/Theophrastus seam; the Socratic sentence; Many and One; and the seed of 23 May 2026. It records the framework's maker-count states in their dates, from no count claimed (#123) through two not established (#1576) and the count left open because uncounted (#1588) to the production model of one self-dividing maker (#1658), held as the governing hypothesis while the reception history (#1733) is documented independently of it. It sets out four evidence bodies, interpretive, stylometric, manuscript-philological and reception-historical, each with its inference limit and its failures, and evaluates the received many-maker reading on the same bodies, finding it established by none and almost wholly unargued.

The machine-traversable component is the holographic kernel, attached as files: positions, records, claims bound to quotations and record hashes, a graph under a relation policy that licenses change on named dimensions only, two timelines, captures, ten lines of research stating what result would advance or retreat the framework and what each moves, and the builder and verifier that rewrite and test it from the archive's registries. Two rounds of reader runs, in which models that had not seen the records rebuilt the framework from the kernel alone, are attached with their scores; the second round's mean yield was 0.977. The hologram was built by Claude (Anthropic) under Lee Sharks's direction, with the Crimson Hexagonal Archive credited as a contributor: it is built from the archive's deposits, protocols and registries.
